issues.issue: The clause says fees are assessed on items that bring the Account "into a negative balance" but also that pending authorizations "reduce your available balance" without incurring a fee, leaving unclear which balance triggers the fee.
It promises "advance notice" of any change in processing order, while the Amendments clause reserves the right to give only such notice "as we determine is appropriate."
Sub-paragraph (e), "we believe is otherwise not properly payable," is an open catch-all sitting against four specific enumerated grounds for refusal.
"Restrictive legend" is illustrated by two examples "and the like," leaving unclear whether ordinary restrictions such as "For Deposit Only" fall within it.

Debits initiated by a party to whom account information was given are "deemed authorized," while the Unauthorized Transfers section gives the customer rights for transfers "made without your permission using information from your check."

An overdraft is defined by funds available "in accordance with the Bank's Funds Availability Policy," but the next clause and the processing-order clause measure overdrafts by the "negative available balance" after deducting pending authorizations.

The $5 daily allowance and the sentence charging "for each transaction that overdraws your account" once the day-end negative balance exceeds $5 do not say whether the transactions within the first $5 are themselves chargeable.

Fee terms are referred out to an "Important Information for Consumers about your TD Bank Checking Account" brochure, which the introductory clause does not list among the documents comprising the Agreement.
A stop payment request must be received "in such timely manner so as to give the Bank a reasonable opportunity to act" and must "precisely identify" five data points, neither standard being fixed.
"Reasonable time" is said to "depend on the circumstances" and then given a one-way safe harbor, leaving it uncertain whether anything slower can ever be reasonable.
It promises recovery of actual loss "up to the face amount of the check," which cannot be reconciled with the Limited Liability clause capping recovery at three months of fees paid.
New fee rules take effect "after the Change Date" while the parallel interest rules take effect "on the day" of the change, leaving the Change Date itself unassigned for fees.

It requires indemnity for losses from legal action "involving you or your Account," including interpleader the Bank itself commences, while the general Indemnity clause excludes "claims that you may assert against us."

"Upon initiation of an interpleader action, we will be relieved and discharged of all further duties and obligations" does not say whether the discharge is limited to the disputed funds or extends to the whole relationship.
The right arises on "any debt you owe us that is in default," but the Agreement defines default only for an Account, not for a debt, leaving the trigger unfixed.
It allows a hold whenever "we have a claim against you," whereas the Right of Set-Off clause conditions the underlying remedy on a debt that is in default.
The security interest covers "your deposit Accounts" without exception, while the Right of Set-Off clause immediately above excludes IRA, Health Savings and Coverdell Accounts.

The cap is subject to anything "expressly prohibited or otherwise restricted by ... this Agreement," a self-referential carve-out that leaves the cap's own reach uncertain, and liability turns on the undefined phrase "bad faith."

The cap of three months' fees cannot be reconciled with the Stop Payments clause promising recovery up to the face amount of the check or with Part IV's "Our Liability" promise of liability for losses or damages.

The disclaimer of any fiduciary or special relationship sits awkwardly with the Trust Account and fiduciary/custody Account provisions, which contemplate the Bank holding accounts in a fiduciary form.
Default arises if "we, in our sole discretion, are not satisfied with your condition or affairs, financial or otherwise," an open-ended trigger appended to seven specific enumerated events.

The waiver reaches actions arising out of "THE DEALINGS OF THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN YOU OR US" — a phrase that is both grammatically defective ("OR" for "AND") and of uncertain scope beyond the Account.
"[F]or any reason, or no reason without notice to you" is punctuated so that it is unclear whether "without notice" qualifies both branches or only the second.

Deeming a zero-balance Account "closed by you" after forty-five days does not sit easily with the Abandoned Accounts clause, which contemplates the Bank holding and escheating funds in unused Accounts.
The Account is made subject to "our usual banking practices" and then to "general commercial banking practices in the area we serve," neither of which is defined or ascertainable from the document.

Subjecting the Account to the Bank's own usual practices is hard to square with the Limited Liability section's statement that the Bank's internal policies and procedures "do not impose on us a higher standard of care."
Governing law is tied to "the Store where you opened your Account," which supplies no answer for Accounts opened online, by mail or by telephone.
The Night Depository Agreement instead applies "the state laws that apply to your primary deposit account," a different and undefined connecting factor.
